text:
Metropolis doesn't walk; it stampedes. Elevated trains thunder above canyons of buff limestone and polished chrome, newsboys shout afternoon extras through exhaust haze, and forty stories overhead, a colossal gilded globe turns lazily atop the Daily Planet building like a second sun tethered to Ninth Street.

Up in the twelfth-floor city room, seventy Underwood typewriters hammer out a steady iron rain. Perry White stalks between desks chomping an unlit Panatela cigar down to wet shreds, bellowing for shipping manifests while teenaged copyboy Jimmy Olsen—all freckles, red cowlick, and crooked green bow tie—dodges flying wastebaskets with wet darkroom prints clipped to his sleeve.

Clark Kent fits into the corner desk near the water cooler almost too well. He hunches two inches out of his true height, speaks half an octave softer than necessary, fumbles revolving doors, and lets sharper reporters raid his pencil cup. Lois Lane, seated six feet away in a razor-cut navy pinstripe suit with a tilted felt hat pinned over dark curls, sizes up Perry's new hire in roughly four seconds and writes him off as harmless Kansas wallpaper.

She has bigger game tonight. Two stories, actually, neither of which Perry wants touching libel court without hard proof: at midnight, Evelyn Curry goes to the electric chair at State Penitentiary for a fatal shooting Lois suspects was committed by brassy nightclub singer Claire, and downtown, sleek munitions lobbyist Alex Greer is quietly bribing Senator Barrows to push through an emergency defense contract tied to black-market exotic weaponry.

"Stick to flower shows, Kent," Lois tosses over her shoulder, snatching her handbag as the five-o'clock whistle blows. "Real news bites."

Clark smiles mildly, adjusts his horn-rimmed glasses, waits until the elevator doors slide shut, and steps calmly out the open twelfth-story washroom window into rushing twilight air.

Earth's yellow sun has soaked into him for twenty-four years now; he doesn't merely leap, as he did in Smallville's pastures—he rides Earth's magnetic lines like a hawk on a thermal, crimson cape snapping clean above harbor tugboats.

By ten-thirty, guided by telescanner vision piercing coastal fog, he intercepts Claire packing steamer trunks aboard a Panama-bound freighter at Pier 9. One look at a six-foot-three stranger in primary colors hovering serenely outside her locked brass porthole drains every drop of bravado from her painted lips; within ten minutes she scribbles a seven-page confession naming her accomplices.

At 11:57 PM, cold rain needles the slate roof of the Governor's Mansion.

Down in the foyer, two state troopers whirl as boots thud softly onto the front veranda. When the tall figure in blue and red ignores their barked warning and grasps the two-inch solid steel security door with bare hands, both troopers open fire with Thompson submachine guns.

Lead slugs flatten like dropped nickels against the crimson S across his chest, tinkling harmlessly onto the parquet floor.

He doesn't strike the troopers. He gently plucks both hot barrels from their hands, knots the steel gun-tubes together like wet licorice, peels the reinforced vault door off its hinges to climb the grand staircase, and deposits a bound, spitting Claire—alongside her signed confession—squarely atop the Governor's quilted bedspread with ninety seconds left before the prison dynamo throws its switch. Leaning against the mahogany bedpost with arms folded, he waits politely until the trembling Governor screams Evelyn Curry's stay of execution into the candlestick telephone, then offers a quiet goodnight and blurs out the open French doors.

Crossing the Lower East Side tenements on his way home, his hearing—tuned too wide, perhaps, in the exhilaration of open sky—catches a woman's sharp cry and the ugly snap of cowhide behind a fourth-floor curtain. Glass shatters inward as he lands between a terrified seamstress and her drunken husband. The brute lunges with a pearl-handled switchblade; steel meets bare collarbone and snaps clean in half. One open-handed shove sends the man through a lath-and-plaster partition into his own icebox—alive, unbroken, and permanently cured of lifting a belt—while the stranger pauses only long enough to drape a fallen wool shawl over the wife's shaking shoulders before leaping back into the mist.

By noon the next day, Metropolis talks of nothing else. A circus acrobat? A Martian? A secret New Deal project?

Lois Lane is furious she missed him, which is probably why she lets mild-mannered Clark talk her into dinner at the Chez Pierre supper club that evening—mostly because she knows lobbyist Alex Greer drinks champagne in the back VIP alcove, and Clark makes a convenient decoy. Halfway through the soup course, Greer's chief enforcer, a thick-necked bruiser named Butch Matson who dislikes reporters eyeing his boss's booth, swagger-steps up to their table, blows cigar smoke in Clark's face, and grabs Lois's wrist for a rumba.

Clark puts on a masterclass in cowardice. He stammers, knocks over a breadbasket, apologizes to Matson's cufflinks, and edges backward toward the coatroom while crimson fury rises up Lois's throat.

Lois slaps Matson clean across the jaw herself, flings her linen napkin into Clark's minestrone, and marches out into the rain, swearing she wouldn't cross a puddle on Clark Kent's coat.

She makes it half a block before tires screech against wet cobblestones. An emerald-green sedan jumps the curb; Matson and three gunmen yank Lois off her heels into the backseat, roaring north onto the winding cliffside asphalt of the Palisades Road to dump nosy Miss Lane into the Hudson.

Two miles past the city limits, Matson's high beams slice the fog—and illuminate two scarlet boots planted wide on the double yellow line.

"Run him flat!" Matson barks.

The driver floors it. Eighty miles an hour. Seventy yards. Twenty.

Hands close beneath the chrome front bumper. Metal shrieks like a slaughtered hog as two tons of Detroit steel stop dead, rear wheels spinning wildly in empty air. Inside the cab, Matson's pistol clatters across the dashboard while Lois presses both palms against the cracked safety glass, scarcely breathing. Effortlessly—almost thoughtfully, as though checking the weight of a melon—the caped man lifts the emerald-green sedan clear above his head, tilts it forty degrees until Matson and his three trigger-men spill howling onto the roadside weeds, and brings the empty automobile smashing nose-first down against a granite boulder in a shower of sparks and radiator steam.

Before Matson's crew can scramble past the ditch, strong arms scoop Lois out of the damp grass. For forty dizzying seconds she smells crisp high-altitude ozone and, strangely enough, clean dry hay, watching harbor lights wheel far beneath her heels before he sets her gently beside a streetcar kiosk near Printing House Square.

"Tell Mr. White," says a warm baritone she almost—though surely not—thinks she has heard before, "that Miss Curry is having breakfast at home."

Up he goes, clearing an elevated railway trestle in a single soaring arc. Two hours later, Lois rips her third sheet out of the roller, types SUPERMAN in forty-point headline caps, and hands Perry White the biggest morning edition since Lindbergh.

AN OPEN LETTER TO GEORGE W. BUSH: TWENTY-FIVE YEARS AFTER 9/11, EXPLAIN “ISLAM IS A RELIGION OF PEACE”

THE EVIDENCE™

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

Dear President Bush:

Your administration repeatedly advanced the declaration that “Islam is a religion of peace.” Your press secretary, Ari Fleischer, explicitly identified it as your position. Twenty-five years after September 11, Americans are entitled to ask what justified that sweeping assurance and how you reconcile it with the continuing violence of organizations invoking Islamic authority.

The wording and chronology deserve precision. At the Islamic Center of Washington on September 17, 2001, your exact words were “Islam is peace.” The longer formulation became an expressly stated administration position. This letter addresses that broader declaration, rather than attributing the longer sentence to your September 17 speech.

You were speaking to a wounded country. Americans had watched people leap from burning buildings. Families were searching for loved ones. The nation needed leadership, an accurate explanation of the enemy, and assurance that the government would protect its citizens.

Your mosque visit addressed another immediate concern. You described Muslim women afraid to leave their homes and reminded Americans that their Muslim neighbors included military personnel, physicians, business owners, and parents. You condemned intimidation against innocent people. That was a legitimate exercise of presidential leadership.

But protecting those citizens did not require you to pronounce a definitive judgment on the nature of Islam. You could have defended their rights, condemned retaliation, and insisted on individual accountability without presenting a sweeping religious conclusion as an established fact.

What qualified your administration to settle which interpretation of Islam was authentic?

YOUR DECLARATION LEFT THE CENTRAL QUESTION UNANSWERED

The terrorists claimed religious justification. You rejected their claim. That rejection expressed a moral judgment, but it did not explain how their interpretation developed, why it attracted followers, or how its influence could be defeated.

Those questions were essential. An ideology does not lose its influence because a president declares that its adherents misunderstand their religion. Its arguments must be examined, its recruitment understood, its organizations disrupted, and its claims challenged.

A useful explanation would have distinguished ordinary Muslim religious practice from Islamist political movements and violent jihadist organizations. Those categories involve different beliefs, conduct, and objectives. The declaration that Islam is a religion of peace offered Americans little help in understanding those distinctions.

YOUR ADMINISTRATION WAS ASKED TO EXPLAIN

This concern was raised while you were president. At an October 16, 2002, press briefing, a reporter challenged the administration’s characterization of Islam, citing passages of the Quran. Fleischer rejected the question’s premise and reaffirmed your position. He then argued against blaming innocent people or an entire religion for terrorists’ actions.

His defense of innocent people addressed collective blame. It did not resolve the underlying question about religious interpretation. Whether a particular passage supports the reporter’s reading requires examination of the text and its context. Reaffirming a presidential belief cannot perform that work.

That distinction remains significant. Defending a citizen against an unsupported accusation and evaluating a religious doctrine are different responsibilities. Your administration repeatedly answered questions about the second by emphasizing the first.

TWENTY-FIVE YEARS LATER, THE THREAT REMAINS

The Institute for Economics & Peace’s Global Terrorism Index 2026 identifies Islamic State, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, and al-Shabaab as the four deadliest terrorist organizations in 2025. Militant Islamist organizations remain central to the international terrorist threat a quarter-century after September 11.

The institute describes Islamic State’s dispersed affiliate network, JNIM’s expansion in the Sahel, the Pakistani Taliban’s resurgence, and al-Shabaab’s persistence despite military pressure. These organizations exploit instability and adapt to changing conditions. Their survival requires an explanation that examines both their ideology and the circumstances enabling their operations.

Their continuing violence does not establish that peaceful interpretations of Islam are insincere or nonexistent. It does establish that a general assurance about peace is insufficient to explain the movements committing that violence.

How did your declaration help Americans understand the religious arguments these organizations use to recruit followers and justify coercion?

THE EVIDENCE REQUIRES HONESTY IN BOTH DIRECTIONS

There is also evidence of improvement. The 2026 index reports that worldwide terrorism deaths declined by 28 percent in 2025. That is significant. An honest assessment must acknowledge progress alongside the persistence of dangerous organizations.

The existence of Islamist terrorism cannot establish the guilt of an individual Muslim. An accusation against a person requires evidence about that person. Religious affiliation alone cannot supply it. Your insistence that innocent Americans should be protected remains defensible.

But the existence of peaceful Muslims does not answer every criticism of Islamic teachings, religious institutions, or movements seeking political power. Personal innocence and institutional scrutiny are separate questions. Neither cancels the other.

Americans should be able to examine religious arguments for violence, restrictions on freedom of conscience, and demands for religious supremacy. Such inquiries require accurate sourcing and careful distinctions. They should receive substantive answers.

Religious freedom includes the freedom to question religion.

WHAT AMERICANS NEEDED TO HEAR

Mr. President, you could have affirmed that Muslim Americans possessed the same rights as everyone else while acknowledging that the attackers belonged to a movement whose religious arguments required serious examination.

You could have explained that the government would assess organizations through evidence about their teachings, financing, affiliations, and conduct. Public professions of peace would be considered alongside what those organizations actually supported.

You could have emphasized that peaceful worship would be protected and that recruitment for violence, threats, and assistance to terrorist organizations would receive scrutiny regardless of the religious language used to justify them.

That approach would have supplied an understandable standard: protect individual rights, investigate specific wrongdoing, and examine the ideology used to excuse it.

The phrase “Islam is a religion of peace” could reassure listeners. By itself, it could not answer their most consequential questions.

THE QUESTIONS STILL BEFORE YOU

Were you describing how peaceful Muslims understood their faith? Were you making a diplomatic statement intended to preserve cooperation? Were you offering a theological judgment? Were you attempting all three?

Those purposes are different. Each requires its own explanation.

Your September 17 speech clearly expressed concern about intimidation. It did not establish that your broad religious conclusion adequately accounted for competing interpretations or the movements acting upon them. Americans can recognize the value of your immediate purpose while challenging the reach of your words.

The record presented here also does not establish that you knowingly lied. That accusation would require evidence of your knowledge and intent. The criticism supported here is more precise: your administration offered a categorical religious assurance that did not adequately explain the enemy’s beliefs and methods.

THE FINDINGS

Your defense of innocent Muslim Americans was justified. Your administration’s declaration that Islam is a religion of peace went beyond defending their rights and provided an insufficient explanation of the ideological threat confronting the country.

Twenty-five years later, lethal Islamist organizations continue to operate. Their persistence requires scrutiny of the doctrines, institutions, networks, and conditions sustaining them. The documented decline in worldwide terrorism deaths also deserves acknowledgment.

Americans deserved leaders capable of defending religious liberty while examining religious claims used to authorize violence. Those responsibilities could—and should—have been fulfilled together.

Mr. President, you offered a memorable assurance. Twenty-five years later, Americans still deserve the explanation.

Respectfully,

Kim Wojcinski

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

COAS DEEPENS ARMY TRANSFORMATION, COMMISSIONS 120 HOMES, PRIORITISES TROOPS’ WELFARE BEYOND SERVICE

Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, the Chief of Army Staff, has reaffirmed the Nigerian Army’s commitment to sustained infrastructural development and improved personnel welfare. This commitment was expressed during the commissioning of 120 newly completed three-bedroom housing units on Friday 13 November 2026 at Idu, Abuja. These units are part of Phase 2 of the Affordable Home Ownership Option for All Soldiers (AHOOAS) and bring the total number of housing units delivered nationwide to 700. This further strengthens efforts to provide soldiers with decent and affordable homes after meritorious service.

COAS emphasized that the Nigerian Army’s ongoing infrastructural development encompasses modern barracks accommodation, healthcare facilities and post-service housing schemes designed to improve troops’ living conditions, boost morale and enhance operational effectiveness. He noted that the Army's transformation agenda places equal premium on combat readiness and personnel welfare, in line with his Soldier-First Culture. He further disclosed that 5 per cent of the housing units have been reserved for personnel wounded in action, reaffirming the Army’s commitment to those who have made enormous sacrifices in defence of the nation.

The COAS noted that the AHOOAS programme has progressively delivered 400 housing units in Abuja in December 2024, 60 in Ibadan in December 2025, 80 in Jos in June 2026 and 40 in Benin City on 6 November 2026, in addition to the newly commissioned 120 units. He commended the Post-Service Housing Development Limited (PHDL), project partners and successive Army leaderships, particularly the late Lieutenant General Taoreed Lagbaja and the current Chief of Defence Staff, General Olufemi Oluyede, for their contributions to the initiative.

Earlier, the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of PHDL, Major General Kevin Ukandu, disclosed that Phase 3 of the Idu housing project is already under construction and scheduled for completion in the first quarter of 2027. He added that the estate features a 2.5-kilometre asphalted road with drainage, a 500KVA transformer, solar-powered streetlights and a water reticulation system, reaffirming PHDL’s commitment to ensuring that more soldiers become homeowners before retirement.

*PMIF26 Concludes with Major Investment Agreements, Pakistan Reaffirms Commitment to Mineral Value Addition*

_The 2-day forum brought together over 10,000 attendees, 122 exhibitors and participation from more than 60 countries_ 

*ISLAMABAD, November 13, 2026:* The two-day Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026 (PMIF26) concluded in Islamabad on Friday with Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif inviting international investors to explore Pakistan’s mineral wealth, assuring them of investment protection and government support, while calling for a shift from exporting raw minerals to developing domestic processing and refining facilities.
Addressing the concluding day of the forum, attended by over 10,000 participants from more than 60 countries, the prime minister declared, “Your safety is our safety,” and pledged to address concerns and facilitate investment in the mining and minerals sector. He stressed that Pakistan must move beyond exporting unprocessed resources and establish facilities to convert raw materials into finished and semi-finished products, generating greater economic value, employment, technical expertise and technology transfer. Referring to a Goldman Sachs projection that Pakistan could become the world’s sixth-largest economy by 2075, PM Shehbaz said he hoped the country would achieve the milestone earlier than 2050.

The prime minister, accompanied by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, also inaugurated the National Minerals Data Centre and the Geological Survey of Pakistan (GSP) GeoPortal. The digital platforms are designed to improve access to geological information, support mineral exploration, reduce uncertainty for investors and facilitate informed investment decisions.

In his address, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir said Pakistan’s ambition extended beyond exporting raw minerals to developing the complete value chain domestically, including refining and manufacturing. He described turning the country’s mineral wealth into tangible economic gains as a collective national goal and stressed that communities in mineral-rich areas must benefit directly from mining projects. He called for long-term partnerships that generate lasting value for Pakistan and its partners, urging the country to move “from potential to production, from promises to action, and from raw exports to value-added growth”.

A major announcement during the forum came from the Frontier Works Organization (FWO), which announced an estimated 350 million tonnes of copper in the Dasht-e-Kain area of Chagai, Balochistan, based on approximately half of its drilling data analysed so far. The announcement highlighted the exploration potential of Pakistan and added to the range of investment opportunities presented during the forum. 

Mari Minerals announced the discovery of its first-ever gold and copper reserves in Chagai. The reserve has a potential of around 1 billion tonnes of copper and gold. The National Resources Limited (NRL) announced a $100 million investment in Pakistan’s mineral sector.

Federal Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik outlined Pakistan's push into critical minerals like copper, gold, lithium, and antimony, emphasizing domestic refining, advanced geological mapping, and infrastructure upgrades like the Rohri-Nokundi railway to link mineral hubs globally.

OGDC President Ahmed Hayat Lak celebrated PMIF26's success in forging international partnerships and launching digital data portals, stressing that execution, technical excellence, and transparent policies are vital to turning mineral wealth into lasting economic progress.

Diverse conference sessions covered AI exploration, infrastructure security, and environmental standards, complemented by an international exhibition where participants signed 13 major agreements and MoUs before concluding with an invitation to the next forum in November 2027.

Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

PMIF26 Concludes with Major Investment Agreements, Pakistan Reaffirms Commitment to Mineral Value Addition

The 2-day forum brought together over 10,000 attendees, 122 exhibitors and participation from more than 60 countries

ISLAMABAD, November 13, 2026: The two-day Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026 (PMIF26) concluded in Islamabad on Friday with Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif inviting international investors to explore Pakistan’s mineral wealth, assuring them of investment protection and government support, while calling for a shift from exporting raw minerals to developing domestic processing and refining facilities.
Addressing the concluding day of the forum, attended by over 10,000 participants from more than 60 countries, the prime minister declared, “Your safety is our safety,” and pledged to address concerns and facilitate investment in the mining and minerals sector. He stressed that Pakistan must move beyond exporting unprocessed resources and establish facilities to convert raw materials into finished and semi-finished products, generating greater economic value, employment, technical expertise and technology transfer. Referring to a Goldman Sachs projection that Pakistan could become the world’s sixth-largest economy by 2075, PM Shehbaz said he hoped the country would achieve the milestone earlier than 2050.

The prime minister, accompanied by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, also inaugurated the National Minerals Data Centre and the Geological Survey of Pakistan (GSP) GeoPortal. The digital platforms are designed to improve access to geological information, support mineral exploration, reduce uncertainty for investors and facilitate informed investment decisions.

In his address, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir said Pakistan’s ambition extended beyond exporting raw minerals to developing the complete value chain domestically, including refining and manufacturing. He described turning the country’s mineral wealth into tangible economic gains as a collective national goal and stressed that communities in mineral-rich areas must benefit directly from mining projects. He called for long-term partnerships that generate lasting value for Pakistan and its partners, urging the country to move “from potential to production, from promises to action, and from raw exports to value-added growth”. He said Pakistan’s resources offered opportunities, while its people remained the strength needed to turn them into results.

A major announcement during the forum came from the Frontier Works Organization (FWO), which announced an estimated 350 million tonnes of copper in the Dasht-e-Kain area of Chagai, Balochistan, based on approximately half of its drilling data analysed so far. The announcement highlighted the exploration potential of Pakistan and added to the range of investment opportunities presented during the forum. 

Mari Minerals announced the discovery of its first-ever gold and copper reserves in Chagai. The reserve has a potential of around 1 billion tonnes of copper and gold. The National Resources Limited (NRL) announced a $100 million investment in Pakistan’s mineral sector.

Federal Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik outlined Pakistan's push into critical minerals like copper, gold, lithium, and antimony, emphasizing domestic refining, advanced geological mapping, and infrastructure upgrades like the Rohri-Nokundi railway to link mineral hubs globally.

OGDC President Ahmed Hayat Lak celebrated PMIF26's success in forging international partnerships and launching digital data portals, stressing that execution, technical excellence, and transparent policies are vital to turning mineral wealth into lasting economic progress.

Global mining leaders, including executives from Barrick Mining, Ivanhoe Mines, and Minmetals, shared international insights on policy certainty and regional cooperation during high-level strategic dialogues.
